spans.assertion: the analysis used 146,028 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues (England, Germany, France, Spain) to test whether referees give more red cards to dark-skin-toned than light-skin-toned players
the primary estimand, adjusted risk difference, is 0.19 percentage points (95% CI -0.06 to 0.43; p=0.142)
the secondary estimand, adjusted odds ratio, is 1.17 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.42; p=0.109)

this difference is not statistically significant and the 95% CI includes zero, so the true effect could range from a 0.06pp decrease to a 0.43pp increase
the point estimate for the adjusted odds ratio is 1.172
the 95% CI for the odds ratio is [0.965, 1.422]

the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad, representing all encounters between a specific player and referee across the season
the total analysis sample is 99,645 dyads
15,990 dyads (16.0%) are classified as dark skin
83,655 dyads (84.0%) are classified as light skin
there are 1,214 unique players in the sample
there are 2,768 unique referees in the sample
there were 1,241 total red cards (1.25% of dyads)
the outcome variable was defined as a binary indicator of whether the player received any red card from that referee across all games in the dyad
dark skin was defined as an average skin tone rating ≥0.75 (normalized), corresponding to original ratings of 4 or 5 on the 5-point scale
light skin was defined as an average skin tone rating ≤0.25 (normalized), corresponding to original ratings of 1 or 2 on the 5-point scale
the skin tone rating used was the average of two independent raters' assessments of player profile photos
all continuous variables were standardized (mean-centered and scaled by SD) for model convergence

the model adjusted for seven covariates: number of games, player position (categorical, Defender reference), player height, player weight, yellow cards, goals scored, and league country (categorical, England reference)
age was excluded from the model because it was missing for 60% of observations, to avoid substantial sample loss and potential selection bias
the primary model used was a Linear Probability Model (OLS regression)
standard errors in the primary model were clustered by player to account for multiple dyads per player
the secondary model used was logistic regression
standard errors in the secondary model were clustered by player
the logistic model was used to calculate the adjusted odds ratio and the alternative risk difference via marginal standardization (g-computation)
standard errors overall were clustered by player (playerShort) to account for non-independence of multiple dyads per player
a complete-case analysis was performed, dropping observations with missing values for the covariates used in the model
the original dataset contained 146,028 dyads
21,407 dyads missing a skin tone rating (no photo) were excluded, leaving 124,621
17,015 dyads with middle skin tone (0.25<tone<0.75) were excluded, leaving 107,606
7,961 dyads missing height, weight, or position were excluded, leaving 99,645
the final analysis sample is 99,645 dyads (68.2% of the original dataset)

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skin players is not supported by the data
the adjusted risk difference (0.19pp) is small relative to the overall red card rate (1.25%)
the 95% CI for the risk difference includes zero, indicating substantial uncertainty about direction and magnitude
the p-value (0.14) exceeds the α=0.05 threshold, providing insufficient evidence to reject the null
the adjusted odds ratio (1.17) also fails to reach significance, with a CI spanning the null value
results are robust to the restricted-sample sensitivity analysis and consistent across the LPM and logistic estimation methods

taking the point estimate at face value, the effect corresponds to about 2 additional red cards per 1,000 dyads (versus a baseline of 12 per 1,000 for light-skin players), a roughly 16% relative increase

spans.note: caveat that the estimate cannot be confidently distinguished from zero and could be negative, null, or positive
blank + Reconciliation with Prior Research subheading

spans.assertion: the unadjusted difference was statistically significant (p=0.048) but was substantially attenuated after adjusting for player position and league, suggesting the raw association may be explained by these structural differences rather than referee bias
the results do not provide convincing evidence of systematic skin-tone bias in red card decisions, though this null finding should not be overinterpreted as definitive proof of no bias

further research with more granular (game/incident-level) data, better measures of player behavior and match context, longitudinal designs, and implicit bias measures linked to specific referees would be needed to more definitively assess whether skin tone influences referee decisions, but this further research was not conducted here
